sources.entry: Testing AMD's Bergamo: Zen 4c Spam - Tests the same-core claim for Zen 4c: cache latency, clock ceiling and core-to-core paths beside clock-matched Zen 4.

summary.title: Testing AMD's Bergamo: Zen 4c Spam
summary.one_liner: AMD's Bergamo doubles core count per chiplet by using density-optimized Zen 4c cores with half the L3 per cluster, and this article measures the resulting memory, cross-socket, core-to-core latency and application performance trade-offs against Zen 4 and VCache variants.
takeaways: Bergamo doubles cores per CCD by using Zen 4c, which keeps the Zen 4 architecture but uses a smaller physical implementation with 16 MB L3 per 8-core CCX instead of 32 MB.
Memory and cross-socket bandwidth are strong (about 360 GB/s DRAM read, over 120 GB/s cross-socket read), but cross-socket latency is about 200 ns and NUMA-aware software is recommended.
Core-to-core latency is about 30-40 ns within a cluster, 100-120 ns across clusters on a socket, and up to about 212 ns across sockets.

In libx264 a Bergamo die was 69.4% ahead of the 7950X3D Zen 4 CCD, while per-cluster at matched clocks Zen 4 was 4.2% faster; in 7-Zip, the vanilla Zen 4 CCX was 36.9% faster per cluster but the Zen 4c CCD was 34.7% faster per die.
The author compares Bergamo's approach with Intel's Sierra Forest E-cores and Ampere One, noting AMD keeps the same ISA across server and client.
summary.summary: The Chips and Cheese article examines AMD's Bergamo server CPU, which uses density-focused Zen 4c cores to reach higher core counts on the Genoa platform. The author tests cache latency, DRAM and cross-socket bandwidth, NUMA behavior, and core-to-core latency, and compares against Broadwell, Westmere, Milan-X, Genoa-X and Sapphire Rapids where data is available. Light benchmarks on a Ryzen 7950X3D with clocks matched to 3.1 GHz compare Zen 4, VCache and Zen 4c clusters using libx264 and 7-Zip. The article closes with a discussion of AMD's strategy versus Intel's Sierra Forest and Ampere One.
